topic: Matrix Exponentials: The Secret to System Evolution
target_audience: University students in Linear Algebra or Differential Equations

sections.title: The Growth Analogy: From Scalars to Matrices
sections.content: Start with the familiar scalar growth equation dx/dt = rx, where the solution is x(t) = e^(rt). Introduce the concept of extending this to systems of variables represented by vectors. Use a split-screen animation showing a single 'growing' circle (scalar) next to a 'stretching and rotating' grid (matrix).
sections.example: A single colony of bacteria growing at a rate 'r' versus a complex ecosystem of two interacting species (predators and prey) whose populations depend on each other through a matrix 'A'.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Taylor Series Bridge
sections.content: Briefly revisit the Taylor Series for e^x. Explain that because we can add and multiply square matrices, we can plug a matrix into this power series. Visually show the summation terms 1 + x + x^2/2! + ... transforming into I + At + (At)^2/2! + ... with matrices visually stacking to form the final result.
sections.example: An animated 'Taylor Machine' where you feed in a scalar value to get a curve, then swap the input for a 2x2 matrix to see the components of the matrix evolve.

sections.title: The Formal Definition of e^(At)
sections.content: Define the matrix exponential e^(At) using the power series. Emphasize that 't' acts as a time scaling factor. Use a graphical representation of a coordinate plane where the basis vectors start to 'flow' along paths determined by the sum of these matrix powers.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Time-Travel Remote' where the button 't' smoothly warps a square grid into a skewed or rotated shape based on the instructions inside matrix A.

sections.title: The Computational Shortcut: Diagonalization
sections.content: Introduce the 'shortcut' for calculating e^(At) when matrix A is diagonalizable (A = PDP^-1). Explain that e^(At) = P * e^(Dt) * P^-1. Graphically show the process: 1. Change basis (P^-1), 2. Scale along axes (e^Dt), 3. Change back (P).
sections.example: A 'Robot Arm' (P) that re-orients a package so a simple 'Stretching Machine' (e^Dt) can work on it, before the arm rotates it back to the original orientation.

sections.title: Geometric Intuition: Rotations and Scaling
sections.content: Show what different types of matrices produce in the exponential. A skew-symmetric matrix leads to a rotation (e^At is an orthogonal matrix), while a diagonal matrix leads to pure scaling. Use an animation of a character 'Vector' traveling in circles or spiraling outward.
sections.example: A compass needle (Vector) spinning in a magnetic field represented by a skew-symmetric matrix, showing continuous rotation as time 't' advances.

sections.title: Application: Solving Linear Systems
sections.content: Connect the math to the ultimate goal: solving the differential equation dx/dt = Ax. The solution is x(t) = e^(At) * x(0). Highlight that the matrix exponential is the 'fundamental solution' that transitions the system from the initial state to any future state.
sections.example: A flight simulator where the joystick input (matrix A) determines how the plane's orientation (x) evolves over time (t) starting from a takeoff position (x0).
